entries.type: complementizer (compound); the same pair is also a manner-and-comparison subordinator and the standalone retort As if!
entries.register: neutral — the formal counterpart of complementizer like
entries.clause: noun clause — complement of a verb of appearance or sensation (seem, look, sound, feel, appear), and of be in the fixed It's not as if frame
entries.pattern: It [seems/looks/sounds/appears] as if [clause]. · [subject] [seems/looks/sounds/feels] as if [clause]. · It [verb of appearance] to [object] as if [clause]. · It's not as if [clause]. · It's not as if [clause], but [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before as if in this use: it stands between a verb and its own complement, and that junction never takes a comma. The comparison as if is the one with a comma rule, and only when it is fronted (As if nothing had happened, he sat down). Deletion tells you which one you have — It seems by itself is unfinished, so that as if clause is an argument and takes no comma; He talks by itself is a whole sentence, so that one is a modifier and can be moved.
variants: as though (interchangeable, a shade more literary)
like (informal)
that after seem and appear (It seems that nobody read it)
entries.meaning: The formal substitute for complementizer like, and the form to reach for the moment the writing stops being conversational. Mood is the detail Americans split on: when the clause is contrary to fact, careful writing keeps the past subjunctive (It looked as if he were joking), and when the situation may well be true the indicative is normal and far commoner (It looks as if the flight is on time). Keep it apart from the manner as if of He talks as if he owns the place: that one modifies a verb the sentence survives without and can be fronted, while this one is an argument and cannot move anywhere.
examples: It seems as if nobody bothered to open the attachment.
It's not as if I had a choice in the matter.
The engine sounds as if something came loose underneath.
I feel as if we skipped a step somewhere in this recipe.
From up here it looks as if the whole street lost power.
It appeared to the auditors as if the invoices had been backdated.

entries.type: complementizer (compound); the same pair is also a manner-and-comparison subordinator
entries.register: neutral to formal — a shade more literary than as if
entries.clause: noun clause — complement of a verb of appearance or sensation (seem, look, sound, feel, appear), and of be in the It's not as though frame
entries.pattern: It [seems/looks/sounds/appears] as though [clause]. · [subject] [seems/looks/sounds/feels] as though [clause]. · It [verb of appearance] to [object] as though [clause]. · It's not as though [clause]. · It's not as though [clause], but [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before as though when it completes a verb of appearance or sensation — the junction between a verb and its complement never takes one. The comparison as though is the one that takes a comma, and only when fronted: As though on cue, the lights came back on. That construction is a modifier, not an argument.
variants: as if (same meaning, commoner in speech)
like (informal)
that after seem and appear
entries.meaning: The near-twin of as if, genuinely interchangeable with it in meaning and differing only in texture: as though reads slightly more literary and is mildly favored after verbs of feeling (It felt as though hours had passed). Like as if, it does double duty — a complementizer when the clause completes seem, look, sound, feel, or appear, and an adverbial of manner when it modifies an ordinary verb (He shrugged as though the whole thing bored him). Only the adverbial one can be fronted, and only the adverbial one ever takes a comma.
examples: It felt as though hours had passed in that waiting room.
It seems as though every form here has to be filed twice.
It's not as though nobody warned us about the fees.
The house looked as though no one had lived there in years.
It sounded as though the furnace kicked on and then quit.
It seemed to everyone in the room as though the decision had already been made.

entries.type: complementizer; the same spelling is also the subordinating conjunction of condition
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect yes-no question)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] if [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] if [clause]. · [imperative verb] if [clause]. · [subject] [verb] if [clause] or not.
entries.punctuation: No comma before if and none inside the clause. Conditional if is the one that takes a comma when its clause is fronted (If it rains, we'll drive); a noun-clause if can never be fronted at all, so no comma question ever arises.
variants: if … or not — the or not can only trail the clause (if he's coming or not), never sit next to if
entries.meaning: The everyday spoken alternative to whether for indirect yes-no questions. It cannot go everywhere whether goes: no if-clause may follow a preposition, precede a to-infinitive, or serve as the subject of a sentence. It is also ambiguous between condition and question — Let me know if he calls can mean "in the event he calls" or "tell me whether he calls" — and swapping in whether is the standard fix. Keep it separate from the conditional if, which is a different word wearing the same three letters: that one heads an adverbial clause the sentence survives without, moves to the front, and takes a comma there; this one is an argument the verb cannot do without and cannot move anywhere.
examples: I don't know if the pharmacy on Third is still open.
She asked if I'd ever driven a stick shift.
Check if the milk's expired before you pour it.
He wondered if anyone had noticed him slip out.
Nobody could tell me if the flight was delayed or not.
See if the hardware store carries that size.

entries.type: complementizer (informal); the same spelling is also a preposition, a comparison subordinator, a verb, a noun, a quotative (she was like, "no way"), and a discourse particle
entries.register: informal — universal in speech, ordinary in fiction and journalism, still corrected in academic and formal business writing
entries.clause: noun clause — complement of a verb of appearance or sensation (seem, look, sound, feel, act), and of be in the fixed It's not like frame
entries.pattern: It [seems/looks/sounds] like [clause]. · [subject] [seems/looks/sounds/feels] like [clause]. · [subject] [verb of acting] like [clause]. · It's not like [clause]. · It's not like [clause], but [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before like and none inside the clause: it stands between a verb and its own complement, and that junction never takes a comma. The discourse particle like is the one that gets commas (It was, like, three hours), and it is a different word entirely.
variants: formal substitutes as if / as though (It seems as though nobody read it)
that after feel and seem (I feel that we're missing a step)
entries.meaning: The complement-clause like, as opposed to the comparison like of She sings like her mother did. The test is whether the clause is an argument: It seems and I feel are unfinishable without what follows, so the like-clause is filling a noun slot, not modifying anything. Americans use it constantly and edited prose still resists it, so the usable rule is to keep it in speech and dialogue and swap in as if, as though, or that the moment the writing turns formal. The It's not like… frame is fixed and idiomatic, and no substitution improves it.
examples: It seems like nobody bothered to open the attachment.
I feel like we skipped a step somewhere in this recipe.
It's not like I had a choice in the matter.
The engine sounds like something came loose underneath.
She acts like she's never seen a parking meter before.
Honestly, it looks like the whole thing was decided before the meeting started.

entries.type: complementizer; the same spelling is also a relative pronoun, a demonstrative determiner and pronoun, and a degree adverb
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause) — subject, object, subject complement, adjective complement, or noun appositive
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] that [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] that [clause]. · That [clause] [verb phrase]. · It [verb] [object] that [clause]. · [noun] that [clause]. · [adjective] that [clause]. · The [noun] is that [clause].
entries.punctuation: Never a comma before complementizer that — He said, that he was tired is an error. A parenthetical inserted right after it takes commas on both sides: He said that, if it rains, they'll cancel. No comma either when the that-clause is a fronted subject: That he lied surprised no one.
variants: zero that — see zero that
entries.meaning: The workhorse of the category: a pure marker that packages a statement into a noun-sized chunk a verb, noun, or adjective can take as its complement. Four different words share the spelling, and only this one is a conjunction. Unlike relative that (the box that came yesterday), it fills no role inside its own clause and leaves no gap, which is exactly why it can usually be deleted; unlike demonstrative that (I said that), it carries no meaning and takes no stress; unlike the degree adverb that (I'm not that hungry), it modifies nothing. Where whether and if introduce a question, that introduces an assertion.
examples: She admitted that she'd forgotten the deadline entirely.
That he never called back tells you everything.
It's obvious that they rehearsed this.
There's a rumor that the plant is closing in March.
I'm just glad that you two finally met.
The problem is that nobody wants to pay for the repairs.

entries.type: complementizer; also the first half of the correlative pair whether … or
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect yes-no question, or alternative question)
entries.pattern: [verb] whether [clause]. · Whether [clause] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] whether [clause]. · [verb] whether to [verb]. · [verb] whether [clause] or [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before whether, none inside the clause, and none after a fronted subject clause: Whether he comes is up to him. A fronted concessive whether … or … clause is a different construction and does take a comma: Whether you like it or not, it's happening.
variants: whether or not
archaic whether or no
entries.meaning: The complementizer of indirect yes-no questions and of stated alternatives, and the neutral choice everywhere if is barred: after a preposition (depends on whether), before an infinitive (whether to go), at the head of a subject clause, and any time if would be misread as a condition. Against that, the difference is settled versus open — I know that she's coming asserts it; I know whether she's coming only claims to have the answer.
examples: It depends entirely on whether the landlord approves the sublet.
I still can't decide whether to drive or fly.
Whether she was joking is anybody's guess.
He asked me whether the offer was still good.
The real question is whether anyone will notice.
We argued about whether to tell him now or wait until Monday.
related: whether to / what to / how to / where to

entries.type: complementizer; also subordinating in its concessive use
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect question); also adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: [verb] whether or not [clause]. · [verb] whether [clause] or not. · Whether or not [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause], whether or not [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use. In the concessive use ("regardless of whether"), a fronted clause takes a comma after it and a trailing one normally takes a comma before it. If or not is not English in either use.
variants: split whether … or not
archaic whether or no
entries.meaning: Two constructions sharing one shape. As a complementizer it is plain whether with the alternative spelled out, and the or not is padding most editors cut. As a concessive it means "no matter whether," and there the or not is structural and cannot be dropped — which is the quick test for telling the two apart.
examples: Let me know whether or not you can make it Saturday.
I asked whether the check had cleared or not.
Whether or not the weather cooperates, the ceremony starts at four.
Nobody has told us whether or not the position is still open.
He's showing up, whether or not anyone invited him.
The board votes tonight on whether or not to renew the lease.

entries.type: complementizer (null)
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause), object or complement only
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] ∅ [clause]. · [adjective] ∅ [clause]. · The [noun] is ∅ [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma, ever — and the missing word makes the wrong comma more tempting: I think, we took a wrong turn is an error, not a pause.
variants: the overt that
entries.meaning: American English drops complementizer that freely after common reporting and mental verbs (say, think, know, hope, feel, guess, bet) and after adjectives (glad, sure, afraid), and the omission is fully standard in speech and in most edited prose. Omission is blocked in five places: when the clause is the sentence's subject (That he lied surprised me), after a noun (the rumor that…), when anything comes between the verb and the clause (He told me yesterday that he'd quit), in the second of two coordinated clauses (He said he was tired and that he wanted to leave), and in fixed frames like the fact that and not that. After heavy reporting verbs — contend, assert, maintain, note — dropping it is possible but reads badly in formal writing.
examples: I think ∅ we took a wrong turn back at the light.
She said ∅ she'd call back after lunch.
Everyone knows ∅ the parking around the stadium is terrible.
I'm just glad ∅ it's over.
He swears ∅ he mailed the check on Monday.
The trouble is ∅ nobody kept the receipts.
related: the thing is / here's the thing
trouble is / problem is / fact is / truth is
no wonder / small wonder / little wonder

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative adverb); the same word is also an exclamative adverb (How quickly this year went!) and, in the comparison family, a manner subordinator
entries.clause: noun clause — embedded wh-question of manner, means, or degree; also a fused relative of manner, and an embedded exclamative
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] how [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] how [clause]. · How [clause] [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] how to [verb]. · [preposition] how [clause]. · [subject] [verb] how [adjective/adverb] [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere — not before how, not inside its clause, and not before a fronted how-clause subject (How she found the address is still a mystery). Statement order inside the clause: I asked how it works, not I asked how does it work.
entries.meaning: Introduces an embedded question about manner, means, or — with an adjective or adverb attached — extent (how long, how much). It also heads a fused relative meaning "the way in which," where it competes with the way that; formal writing prefers how to the redundant the way how, which is not standard. A third use embeds an exclamative rather than a question — It's amazing how quickly kids pick it up — and that clause, like the others, keeps statement order and ends the sentence with a period.
examples: Nobody ever explained how the billing cycle actually works.
How she found the address is still a mystery to me.
I never learned how to parallel park.
It depends on how much overtime they approve.
Watch how he shifts his grip on the second swing.
She wanted to know how long the drive takes.
It's amazing how fast that dog learned the fence line.
related: whether to / what to / how to / where to

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative phrase)
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question of reason)
entries.pattern: How come [clause]? · [subject] [verb] how come [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [object] how come [clause]. · [imperative verb] [indirect object] how come [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma. Unlike why, how come never triggers inversion even in a direct question: How come he left?, never How come did he leave? A direct question with it still takes a question mark; an embedded one still takes a period (She never explained how come she quit.).
entries.meaning: A colloquial why that takes statement word order in main clauses as well as embedded ones, which makes it the one wh-question American learners can never get inverted by mistake. Its embedded use (I don't know how come) is common in speech and avoided in edited writing, where why is the safe substitute. It also refuses the to-infinitive that most wh-words allow: how come to leave is not English.
examples: How come nobody told me the meeting moved?
I have no idea how come the charge showed up twice.
She never explained how come she quit so suddenly.
"How come you're up so early?" "Couldn't sleep."
Ask him how come the car's still in the shop.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative pronoun and determiner; also fused relative pronoun and exclamative determiner)
entries.clause: noun clause — embedded wh-question, fused ("headless") relative, or embedded exclamative
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] what [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] what [clause]. · What [clause] [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] what to [verb]. · [preposition] what [clause]. · [subject] [verb] what [noun] [clause]. · [subject] [verb] what a [noun] [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma, and none before a fronted what-clause subject: What he said surprised us. Never follow it with that: what that he wants is not English.
entries.meaning: Three jobs in one word. As an interrogative it heads an indirect question (I asked what he wants); as a fused relative it means "the thing(s) which" and needs no antecedent (What he wants is a raise); as an exclamative determiner it embeds the same way an exclamation does, minus the exclamation point (What a mess this is! → You wouldn't believe what a mess this is). The fused-relative use is where learners overreach: what replaces an entire noun-plus-relative sequence, so the thing what he wants and everything what I own are both wrong — after an expressed noun you need that or which, and the what relative of the man what fixed the roof is dialect, not standard American English.
examples: I never found out what the second envelope contained.
What really bothers me is the tone of the email.
Tell me what you need and I'll grab it on the way.
She has no idea what to wear to a rehearsal dinner.
The final bill depends on what the inspector finds.
What he said and what he meant were two very different things.
You wouldn't believe what a mess the kitchen was when we got home.
related: whether to / what to / how to / where to

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative adverb); the same word is also a subordinating conjunction of time, a concessive subordinator, and a relative adverb
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question of time) — distinct from the adverbial when of the time-clause family
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] when [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] when [clause]. · When [clause] [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] when to [verb]. · [preposition] when [clause]. · [linking verb] when [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, including when the clause is a fronted subject: When they'll announce it is anyone's guess. Adverbial when is the one that takes a comma when fronted: When they announce it, we'll know.
entries.meaning: One word, two grammars. In the noun-clause use the when-clause is an argument — substitute something and the sentence still stands — and it never takes a comma; in the adverbial use it modifies the main clause and follows the ordinary fronted-subordinator comma rule. There is also a tense test: the noun clause allows a future (I don't know when he'll arrive), while the adverbial one forbids it (when he arrives, not when he will arrive).
examples: Nobody will tell me when the results get posted.
When the renovation actually finishes is anybody's guess.
She's still deciding when to give notice.
The whole schedule hinges on when the permit clears.
Ask the dispatcher when the next bus comes through.
I honestly don't know when he'll get here.
The only real question now is when they'll announce it.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative adverb; also fused relative); the same word is a place subordinator, a relative adverb, and a concessive subordinator elsewhere
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question of place); also a fused relative of place
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] where [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] where [clause]. · Where [clause] [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] where to [verb]. · [preposition] where [clause]. · [linking verb] where [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before where, none inside the clause, and none after a fronted where-clause subject: Where the money went has never been explained. Adverbial where is the one with a comma rule when fronted (Where the sidewalk ends, the gravel starts). Statement order: I asked where it is, not I asked where is it.
entries.meaning: Heads an embedded question about place, and also a fused relative meaning "the place at which" (This is where I grew up). Distinguish it from the adverbial where of Sit where you like, which modifies the verb rather than filling an argument slot and belongs to the place-clause family, not to this one.
examples: She wouldn't say where she'd been all afternoon.
Where the money actually went has never been explained.
We spent an hour arguing about where to put the couch.
That bend in the road is where the fault line runs.
Text me where you parked so I'm not circling the lot.
It matters a great deal where the closing takes place.
related: whether to / what to / how to / where to

entries.term: whether to / what to / how to / where to
entries.respell: WEH-thur tuh, WUHT tuh, HOW tuh, WAIR tuh
entries.type: complementizer + infinitive marker (infinitival wh-clause); each member is one of the wh-words in this section, or whether, followed by bare to
entries.clause: noun clause (infinitival embedded question) — object of a verb, object of a preposition, subject, or subject complement
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] [wh-word] to [verb]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] [wh-word] to [verb]. · [Wh-word] to [verb] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] [wh-word] to [verb]. · [linking verb] [wh-word] to [verb]. · [subject] [verb] whether to [verb] or to [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere, and no subject inside the clause — the whole point of the construction is that the subject goes unexpressed and is recovered from the main clause. Never add should on top of the to (what to do or what I should do, never what to should do), and never insert that (how to fix it, not how that to fix it).
variants: the finite paraphrase with should or can (where to park → where I should park)
whether or not to (whether or not to sign)
who to — the ordinary American form, where the stiffest prose writes whom to
entries.meaning: The infinitival half of the embedded-question system: the wh-word supplies the question, to supplies a verb with no tense, and the subject is left out and read off the main clause — She's deciding whether to go can only mean she is deciding about herself. It is open to whether and to every wh-word in this section except why and how come (why to go and how come to leave are not English), and it is the one embedded question that sits comfortably after a preposition (a question of what to charge). What it buys is compression: nobody told us where to file it says in six words what nobody told us where we were supposed to file it needs ten to say.
examples: She still hasn't decided whether to take the job or stay put.
Nobody told us where to drop off the paperwork.
He's never learned how to back a trailer down a driveway.
What to wear to the rehearsal dinner turned into a two-day argument.
The real problem is who to call at eleven o'clock on a Sunday night.
Half the meeting went to arguing about whether to renew the contract or to rebid it.
The manual says nothing about which to replace first.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative pronoun or determiner); the same word is also a relative pronoun, restrictive and nonrestrictive
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question, selective)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] which [clause]. · [subject] [verb] which [noun] [clause]. · [subject] [verb] which of [noun phrase] [clause]. · [subject] [verb] which ([noun]) to [verb]. · Which [noun] [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · Which [noun] [subject] [verb] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] which [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use. Relative which is the one with comma rules (the car, which was new, wouldn't start); the noun-clause which never takes one, no matter how long the clause runs.
entries.meaning: The selective interrogative: it asks for a choice from a known, closed set, where what asks open-endedly. I don't know which he picked presumes a menu; I don't know what he picked does not. It works alone or with a noun attached (which flight, which switch).
examples: He wouldn't tell me which of the two offers he'd accepted.
I can never remember which switch runs the porch light.
Which candidate they endorse will decide the primary.
She's still weighing which to keep and which to sell.
The label doesn't say which ingredient causes the reaction.
Which team wins tonight decides the whole bracket.
Everything now depends on which version they actually installed.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative pronoun); the same word is also a relative pronoun
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question, personal)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] who [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] who [subject] [verb]. · [subject] [verb] who to [verb]. · Who [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · It [linking verb] [adjective] who [clause]. · [preposition] who [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma, and statement order: I asked who he is, not I asked who is he. When who is itself the subject of the embedded clause, nothing shifts — I asked who called already looks like a statement. Relative who is the one with a comma rule: nonrestrictive, it takes commas on both sides (my brother, who lives in Denver, called); restrictive, it takes none (the neighbor who called).
entries.meaning: Heads an embedded question about a person. In everyday American English it also covers the object slot that formal grammar reserves for whom (I don't know who they picked), and only the stiffest prose insists otherwise. Distinguish it from relative who, which requires an antecedent noun (the woman who called) and is a relative pronoun, not a conjunction.
examples: Nobody could tell me who signed off on the invoice.
Who leaked the memo is now the only question anyone cares about.
I forget who was supposed to bring the ice.
She asked who I'd been talking to out in the hallway.
It's still unclear who has the authority to cancel the order.
I never did figure out who to send the complaint to.
The whole seating chart depends on who actually shows up.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative pronoun, objective case); the same word is also an objective relative pronoun
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question, personal, object function)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] whom [subject] [verb]. · [subject] [verb] whom [subject] [verb] … [preposition]. · [subject] [verb] [preposition] whom [subject] [verb]. · [subject] [verb] whom to [verb]. · Whom [subject] [verb] [verb phrase]. · It [linking verb] [adjective] whom [subject] [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma, including before a fronted whom-clause subject: Whom they ultimately choose is up to the board. Relative whom is the one with a comma rule — nonrestrictive, it takes commas (the director, whom nobody had met, sat in back); restrictive, none. The case test is substitution inside the clause: if him or her fits, whom is correct (they hired him → I know whom they hired).
entries.meaning: The object form of who, and genuinely formal in American English rather than merely careful. It survives mainly right after a preposition (to whom, for whom, with whom); everywhere else who is the ordinary spoken choice, and a whom pressed into subject position (the man whom I think is guilty) reads as an overcorrection.
examples: I have no idea whom the committee actually interviewed.
The report doesn't say whom the funds were paid to.
Whom they ultimately choose is up to the board.
She asked to whom she should address the appeal.
It remains unsettled whom the estate names as executor.
The style guide never says whom to credit when two people wrote the piece.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative determiner); the same word is also a possessive relative determiner
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question, possessive)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] whose [noun] [verb phrase]. · [subject] [verb] whose [noun] [subject] [verb]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] whose [noun] [clause]. · Whose [noun] [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · [linking verb] whose [noun] [clause]. · [preposition] whose [noun] [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere in the noun-clause use, including before a fronted whose-clause subject: Whose signature is on the second page turned out to matter. Relative whose is the one with a comma rule — nonrestrictive, it takes commas (the tenant, whose lease was up, moved out); restrictive, none. And no apostrophe in either: whose is the possessive, who's is who is or who has. The two are pronounced identically, so this is a writing error rather than a speaking one.
entries.meaning: Asks which person something belongs to, and it always leads a noun (whose car, whose idea, whose turn). Relative whose does the same possessive work inside a modifying clause (the man whose car got towed); the noun-clause whose is the one that answers a question rather than identifying a noun.
examples: Nobody knew whose car was blocking the loading dock.
Whose signature is on the second page turned out to matter enormously.
She wouldn't say whose idea the whole trip had been.
It all depends on whose insurance covers the rental.
The clerk asked whose name the account was under.
Nobody told us whose budget the overtime was coming out of.
The only real question now is whose name goes on the deed.

entries.type: complementizer (interrogative adverb); the same spelling is also a relative adverb after reason and, in older and regional speech, an interjection (Why, of course)
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question of reason)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb] why [clause]. · [subject] [verb] [indirect object] why [clause]. · Why [clause] [verb phrase]. · [linking verb] why [clause]. · [preposition] why [clause]. · the reason why [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma, and no question mark on the containing sentence: I asked why he left. is a statement and ends with a period. The interjection why is the only one of these spellings that takes a comma, and it takes one always: Why, I hadn't thought of that.
entries.meaning: The only wh-word here with no adverbial twin — a why-clause is always a noun clause, which is why it never needs a comma under any arrangement. It is also the one wh-word that refuses a to-infinitive: what to do and how to ask are fine, but why to go is not English, and only the fixed why not takes a bare verb (Why not ask her?).
examples: He never explained why the shipment ran two weeks late.
Why they scheduled it on a holiday weekend is beyond me.
I'd genuinely like to understand why this keeps happening.
That is exactly why I stopped answering his calls.
Nobody thought to ask why the office was empty at noon.
Nobody ever gave us the reason why the account was frozen.
It all comes down to why he waited three weeks to say anything.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); a homograph of the conjunctive adverb however ("nevertheless"), which is a different word with the opposite punctuation
entries.clause: noun clause or adverbial clause of manner (fused relative, "in whatever way"); also concessive ("no matter how")
entries.pattern: [main clause] however [clause]. · However [clause], [main clause]. · However [adjective/adverb] [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] however [adjective/adverb] [clause]. · However [clause] [verb phrase]. · However [adjective/adverb] [clause] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] however [clause].
entries.punctuation: This however punctuates like any other subordinator: no comma when its clause follows the main clause (Do it however you like), and a comma after the clause when it is fronted in the "no matter how" sense (However carefully you write it, he'll find something). No comma ever goes right after the word itself. That pointing belongs to the conjunctive adverb however, which is a different word and takes the opposite treatment: joining two independent clauses it requires a semicolon or a period before it and a comma after it — We left early; however, the traffic was already bad. Putting a comma where that semicolon belongs is a comma splice, not a stylistic choice: We left early, however, the traffic was already bad. is an error.
entries.meaning: A fused relative meaning "in whatever way" or "no matter how," spelled and pronounced exactly like the conjunctive adverb but punctuated the opposite way — a swap that produces one of the most common comma errors in American writing. Two tests separate them. Substitution: if no matter how or in whatever way fits, it is this word; if nevertheless fits, it is the adverb. Movement: the conjunctive adverb slides freely around inside its own clause (The traffic, however, was already bad), while this however is welded to the front of the clause it introduces and cannot move at all.
examples: Do it however you like — I really don't have a preference.
However carefully you write it, he'll find something to fix.
She dresses however she feels when she gets up.
However long it takes is however long it takes.
The system sorts the files however the last user configured it.
She'll finish the job however long it takes.
The refund gets calculated based on however the agent coded the ticket.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); the same word is also a determiner, a concessive subordinator, and a standalone dismissive interjection
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative); also adverbial clause of concessive condition
entries.pattern: [verb] whatever [clause]. · Whatever [clause] [verb phrase]. · [verb] whatever [noun] [clause]. · [preposition] whatever [clause]. · [preposition] whatever [noun] [clause]. · Whatever [clause], [main clause]. · Whatever [noun] [clause], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, including as a fronted subject: Whatever she paid was too much. A fronted "no matter what" clause does take a comma: Whatever happens, call me.
variants: whatsoever (emphatic, and only after a negated noun — no reason whatsoever — never a clause introducer)
entries.meaning: Means "anything that" when it fills a noun slot and "no matter what" when it modifies the main clause, and the comma is the only visible difference between the two. It can also work as a determiner with a noun attached (whatever excuse he gives). The standalone dismissive Whatever. is an interjection and has nothing to do with this entry.
examples: Order whatever looks good to you.
Whatever she paid for that couch, it was too much.
He agrees with whatever the last person in the room said.
Whatever excuse he comes up with, don't fall for it.
I'll take whatever is left once the deposit clears.
Whatever happens tomorrow, we've done what we could.
She'll go along with whatever plan the committee settles on.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); the same word is far more often a subordinating conjunction of time, and it also runs concessive ("no matter when")
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative of time); more often an adverbial clause of time
entries.pattern: [verb] whenever [clause]. · Whenever [clause] [verb phrase]. · Whenever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] whenever [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use. As a time adverbial, a comma after the clause when it is fronted and no comma when it trails — the ordinary subordinator rule.
entries.meaning: Mostly a time adverbial meaning "every time that" or "at any time that," but it does head genuine noun clauses in subject and object position: Whenever he shows up is fine with me. Against when, it trades a specific point in time for an open one — I'll leave when it stops names an occasion, I'll leave whenever it stops accepts any.
examples: Whenever he finally shows up is fine with me.
Pick whenever works best for your schedule.
She calls whenever something in the house breaks.
Whenever you're ready, we'll get started.
The meeting can be whenever the conference room is free.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); the same word is also a subordinating conjunction of place and a concessive ("no matter where")
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative of place); also adverbial clause of place
entries.pattern: [verb] wherever [clause]. · Wherever [clause] [verb phrase]. · Wherever [clause], [main clause]. · [main clause] wherever [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use. A fronted "no matter where" clause takes a comma; a trailing place clause takes none.
entries.meaning: "Any place that" or "no matter where." It heads a noun clause when it fills an argument slot (Wherever they put it is fine) and a place adverbial when it modifies the verb (Sit wherever you like). Against where, it is the indifferent option — where names a place, wherever declines to.
examples: Wherever they end up moving is fine with me.
We'll ship it wherever you need it delivered.
Wherever you go this weekend, take the charger.
He seems to make friends wherever he lands.
The reception drops out wherever the trees get thick.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); the same word is also a determiner and a concessive subordinator
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative, selective)
entries.pattern: [verb] whichever [clause]. · [verb] whichever [noun] [clause]. · Whichever [clause] [verb phrase]. · Whichever [noun] [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · Whichever [clause], [main clause]. · Whichever [noun] [clause], [main clause]. · [preposition] whichever [clause]. · [noun phrase] or [noun phrase], whichever [verb phrase].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, in any position — not even when the clause is a fronted subject (Whichever vendor bids lowest gets the contract). Two other constructions do take one. A fronted concessive ("no matter which") takes a comma before the main clause: Whichever route the driver takes, we're going to hit traffic. And the fixed summarizing tag whichever comes first is set off by a comma from the list it closes: three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
entries.meaning: The selective -ever form: "any one of these that." It presumes a defined set where whatever is open-ended — whichever you want offers a menu, whatever you want offers the world. It is standard boilerplate in contracts and warranties in the tags whichever comes first and whichever is greater.
examples: Take whichever seat you want; they're all the same price.
Whichever vendor bids lowest gets the contract.
She'll be happy with whichever one you pick out.
The warranty expires after three years or 36,000 miles, whichever comes first.
I'll go with whichever is cheaper to ship.
Whichever route the driver takes, we're going to hit traffic.
Whichever they end up choosing, somebody on the committee is going to complain.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative); the same word also heads concessive adverbials ("no matter who")
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative, personal)
entries.pattern: Whoever [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · [verb] whoever [verb phrase]. · [verb] [indirect object] whoever [verb phrase]. · [preposition] whoever [verb phrase]. · [linking verb] whoever [verb phrase]. · Whoever [verb phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, in any position — a fronted subject clause takes none (Whoever parked in my spot is about to get towed), and neither does one sitting after a verb or a preposition. The concessive ("no matter who") is the one comma: fronted, its clause is closed off before the main clause arrives — Whoever ends up with the account, the deadline doesn't move. The case rule matters far more than any comma here: use whoever, not whomever, whenever it is the subject of its own clause — even directly after a preposition, as in Give it to whoever wants it.
entries.meaning: "The person who" or "anyone who." A whole clause, not a bare pronoun, is what follows a preposition, so the preposition never reaches inside to force whomever; choosing the case by looking at the word to the left is the single most common error in this entry. If a verb comes right after, you want whoever.
examples: Whoever parked in my spot is about to get towed.
Give the extra ticket to whoever asks for it first.
I'd like to thank whoever shoveled the front walk.
Whoever wrote this manual has clearly never used the product.
She'll hire whoever can start on Monday.
Whoever ends up with the account, the deadline doesn't move.
The new supervisor will be whoever survives the reorganization.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative, objective case); like whoever, it also heads concessive adverbials ("no matter whom")
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative, personal, object function); also adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: [verb] whomever [subject] [verb]. · [verb] [indirect object] whomever [subject] [verb]. · [preposition] whomever [subject] [verb]. · Whomever [subject] [verb] [verb phrase]. · [linking verb] whomever [subject] [verb]. · Whomever [subject] [verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, including as a fronted subject: Whomever they nominate will face a tough confirmation. The concessive is the one that takes a comma, and only when fronted: Whomever the board picks, the union is going to push back. Use the word at all only when it is the object inside its own clause; substitute him to check — the client designates him → whomever the client designates.
entries.meaning: The object form of whoever, and formal even by whom's standards. Americans overcorrect to it after prepositions, where whoever is usually the right form; the reliable signal is what comes next — a subject and verb call for whomever, a bare verb calls for whoever.
examples: Send the invoice to whomever the client designates.
Whomever they nominate will face a tough confirmation.
She'll work with whomever management assigns her.
Address the letter to whomever you spoke with last week.
The prize goes to whomever the judges rank highest.
Whomever the board picks, the union is going to push back.
The new liaison will be whomever the two departments can agree on.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative, emphatic, objective case); the object form of whosoever, and like it a concessive subordinator ("no matter whom")
entries.register: archaic — confined to legal and testamentary drafting, formal boilerplate, and King James English; never a neutral choice
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative, personal, object function); also adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: [verb] whomsoever [subject] [verb]. · [preposition] whomsoever [subject] [verb]. · Whomsoever [subject] [verb] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] whomsoever it may [verb]. · Whomsoever [subject] [verb], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, including as a fronted subject: Whomsoever the executor names takes the residue. A fronted concessive takes a comma before the main clause: Whomsoever the court appoints, the estate pays the fee. Case is settled inside the clause, exactly as with whomever: whomsoever only when a subject and verb follow it, whosoever when a verb follows directly — to whomsoever it may concern is right, to whomsoever comes first is not.
variants: whosoever (subjective)
the parallel -soever forms whatsoever, whichsoever, wheresoever, howsoever
entries.meaning: The object partner of whosoever, and the -soever form Americans are likeliest to have met, since the boilerplate to whom it may concern keeps its longer cousin in circulation. Nothing in modern prose needs it — whomever is already formal and whoever covers the ordinary cases — and the one thing to get right is that the preposition in front of it governs the whole clause, not the pronoun, so the case is decided by what follows the word rather than what precedes it. Drafters who reach for it as a general-purpose upgrade produce the standard hypercorrection: to whomsoever shall apply should be to whosoever shall apply.
examples: The estate shall be distributed to whomsoever the executor designates.
Whomsoever the parties later substitute assumes every obligation under this clause.
The letter was addressed, half in earnest, to whomsoever it might concern.
He vowed to hand the deed to whomsoever his father had named in the will.
Whomsoever the board may choose, the appointment still requires a public hearing.
The trustee may pay the income to whomsoever the beneficiary directs in writing.

entries.type: complementizer (fused relative, emphatic); whomsoever is its objective form
entries.register: archaic — alive only in legal drafting, hymnody, and King James English; never a neutral choice
entries.clause: noun clause (fused relative, personal, universal); also adverbial clause of concession
entries.pattern: Whosoever [verb phrase] [verb phrase]. · [verb] whosoever [verb phrase]. · [preposition] whosoever [verb phrase]. · [linking verb] whosoever [verb phrase]. · [preposition] whomsoever [subject] [verb]. · Whosoever [verb phrase], [main clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma in the noun-clause use, in any position, including as a fronted subject: Whosoever enters these gates leaves his rank at the door. A fronted concessive is the exception, as everywhere else in this section: Whosoever holds the office, the duties do not change. The case rule is whoever's exactly: whosoever when it is the subject of its own clause, whomsoever only when it is the object inside that clause — so to whomsoever it may concern is right and to whomsoever comes first is not.
variants: whomsoever (objective)
the parallel -soever forms whatsoever, whichsoever, wheresoever, howsoever
entries.meaning: The emphatic whoever, built with the old intensifying suffix -soever, meaning what whoever means with the universality underlined: "any person at all who." Nothing in modern American English needs it — whoever covers every use — and reaching for it in ordinary prose reads as costume. It survives for two reasons: estate and contract drafters want language with no seams in it, and the King James Bible fixed whosoever believeth permanently in the ear of the language.
examples: Whosoever presents this note is entitled to payment in full.
The trust pays out to whosoever survives the settlor.
Address the notice to whomsoever the court appoints.
Whosoever enters these gates leaves his rank at the door.
He promised the reward to whosoever found the dog.
Blessed is whosoever keeps the faith to the end.
Whosoever holds the office, the duties do not change.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal); the same two words also close the causal frames seeing as how and being as how
entries.register: regional and dialectal — Southern, Appalachian, and Midland American speech, plus the folksy narrative voice that imitates it; not standard in edited writing
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause) after a verb of saying, thinking, or conceding
entries.pattern: [subject] allow / reckon / figure / say as how [clause]. · [subject] [verb of saying] [indirect object] as how [clause]. · [subject] allowed as how [clause], [coordinated clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before as how, none between the two words, and none inside the clause — it stands between a verb and its own complement. Causal seeing as how is the one with a comma rule, and only when its clause is fronted (Seeing as how you've done this before, you go first); that phrase belongs to the cause family, not to this one.
variants: the fixed verb frames it lives in: allow as how, reckon as how, figure as how, say as how
plain that or zero that in standard prose (He allowed that it might rain)
entries.meaning: A dialectal that: after allow, reckon, figure, and say it marks a plain statement and keeps no trace of manner, exactly as how that did in Early Modern English. The giveaway is that how has been bleached out of it — He allowed as how it might rain reports what he said, not the way he said it, so the how can be neither questioned nor answered. Keep it apart from causal seeing as how and being as how, which mean "since" and modify the main clause instead of filling a slot in it; in writing, both words simply come out.
examples: He allowed as how the price seemed a little steep for a used mower.
She reckoned as how the storm would blow through before supper.
The foreman said as how they'd be two hands short all week.
Granddad finally admitted as how he'd never actually read the manual.
I figured as how nobody would miss one folding chair.
He allowed as how he might come by Sunday, though he wouldn't promise.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal); as to is also a compound preposition in front of a noun phrase (as to the cost)
entries.register: formal — the register of contracts, memos, and administrative prose
entries.clause: noun clause (embedded wh-question) — complement of a noun or an adjective, occasionally of a verb
entries.pattern: [noun] as to [wh-word] [clause]. · [adjective] as to [wh-word] [clause]. · [verb] as to [wh-word] [clause]. · [determiner] [noun] as to [wh-word] [clause] [verb phrase]. · [noun/adjective] as to [wh-word] to [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it, between its two words, or after its clause — not even when the whole as to phrase is buried inside the subject of the sentence. It never fronts, so the fronted-subordinator comma is never in play.
variants: as to whether — the commonest instance, with an entry of its own
as to + noun phrase (guidance as to the deadline)
the plainer about, of, on, over (a question about what it costs)
entries.meaning: The general frame that as to whether is one case of. English will not park a bare wh-clause after most nouns and adjectives, and as to supplies the missing preposition: a question as to what caused the delay, silent as to who owns the strip, vague as to when it happened. It earns its keep after nouns and adjectives that govern no preposition of their own; after a plain verb it is padding, since He inquired as to what it cost says nothing that He asked what it cost does not. Where an ordinary preposition already fits — about, on, over — that preposition is the better word, and as to reads as officialese.
examples: The deed is silent as to who maintains the shared driveway.
There was some confusion as to what the deposit actually covered.
Nobody could give us guidance as to how the surcharge gets calculated.
Her testimony was vague as to when the second call came in.
A dispute as to which company owned the easement stalled the sale for a year.
The bylaws say nothing as to how many proxies one member may hold.
The committee is still undecided as to whom the award should honor.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.clause: noun clause (indirect yes-no question)
entries.pattern: [noun] as to whether [clause]. · [adjective] as to whether [clause]. · [verb] as to whether [clause]. · [determiner] [noun] as to whether [clause] [verb phrase]. · [noun/adjective] as to whether [clause] or [clause]. · [noun/adjective] as to whether to [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma before it, inside it, or after its clause — not even when the whole as to whether clause is packed inside the subject of the sentence (A dispute as to whether the easement runs with the land has held up the closing). It never fronts, so no fronted-subordinator comma is ever in play.
variants: as to (+ wh-) — the same frame with the other wh-words (as to what, as to how, as to who, as to which)
as to + noun phrase (as to the cost)
entries.meaning: A formal connector for the spots where a noun or adjective needs a preposition in front of a whether-clause: doubt as to whether, silent as to whether, a question as to whether. After a plain verb it is padding — He questioned as to whether is simply worse than He questioned whether — so the usable rule is to keep it after nouns and adjectives and delete it after verbs.
examples: There is some doubt as to whether the signature is genuine.
The contract is silent as to whether renewals are automatic.
The memo raised a question as to whether the policy still applies.
Opinions differ sharply as to whether the fee is refundable.
He gave no guidance as to whether we should keep the originals.
A dispute as to whether the easement runs with the land has held up the closing for months.
The panel was divided as to whether to reopen the case or let the ruling stand.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.register: archaic, surviving in legal and literary prose
entries.clause: noun clause after a negated verb or noun of doubting or denying
entries.pattern: [negated verb of doubt/denial] but that [clause]. · There is no [doubt/question] but that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma. Do not confuse it with the ordinary sequence but + a that-clause (I know he's late, but that isn't the issue), where but coordinates and that starts a fresh clause — that one does take the coordinating comma.
variants: bare but in the same frame (I don't doubt but he'll come)
but what (regional and dialectal)
entries.meaning: An old negative complementizer meaning roughly "that … not," alive today only after doubt, deny, and question in the negative. Contemporary American English uses a plain that: I don't doubt that he acted in good faith. Note the built-in double negative that makes it read backwards to modern eyes — I never doubted but that she'd win means the speaker expected her to win.
examples: I do not doubt but that he acted in good faith.
There is no question but that the notice was properly served.
She never denied but that the money had changed hands.
It cannot be denied but that the practice was widespread at the time.
Who knows but that he was right all along?

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.register: regional and dialectal — Southern, Appalachian, and Midland American speech; not standard in edited writing anywhere
entries.clause: noun clause after a negated verb or noun of doubting, denying, or knowing
entries.pattern: [negated verb of doubt/denial] but what [clause]. · There is no [doubt/question] but what [clause]. · It won't be long but what [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma, exactly as with but that. Do not confuse it with the ordinary coordination but + what-clause (I heard the story, but what he actually meant was different), where but joins two independent clauses and therefore does take a comma before it.
variants: but that (the older and more literary form)
bare but (I don't doubt but he'll come)
entries.meaning: The spoken cousin of but that, and the form far more Americans have actually heard: I don't doubt but what she'll be there, There's no question but what he knew. It carries the same built-in double negative — I never doubted but what she'd win means the speaker expected her to win — and the same restriction to negated verbs of doubting and denying. Dictionaries mark it dialectal rather than archaic, which is the real difference from but that: this one is alive, just not in print. In writing, use a plain that.
examples: I don't doubt but what she'll be there before we are.
There's no question but what he knew about the leak.
It won't be long but what somebody notices the sign is gone.
Nobody denied but what the road needed paving.
I wouldn't be surprised but what they close the store by fall.

entries.type: complementizer (infinitival for … to); the same spelling is also a coordinating conjunction meaning "because" and one of the most common prepositions in the language
entries.clause: noun clause (infinitival clause with an overt subject)
entries.pattern: For [subject] to [verb] [verb phrase]. · [verb] for [subject] to [verb]. · It [verb] for [subject] to [verb]. · [adjective] for [subject] to [verb]. · [noun] for [subject] to [verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma between for and its subject and none before to. A fronted for-clause subject takes no comma either: For him to say that was out of line. The coordinating for meaning "because" is the one with a comma rule — joining two independent clauses, it takes a comma before it: We turned back, for the road was washed out. The preposition takes none at all.
variants: for … to — the full name of the frame, since the two words function as one discontinuous complementizer and neither half stands without the other
bare to + verb when the subject is understood from context (It's hard to say)
entries.meaning: The complementizer that lets an infinitive clause carry its own subject: for marks the subject, to marks the verb, and the pair wraps a whole clause into a noun slot. It is neither the coordinating for meaning "because" nor the ordinary preposition — the test is that a to-infinitive always follows. Its subject takes object case: for him to go, never for he to go.
examples: For him to apologize now would surprise everyone.
It's important for the kids to hear it from you first.
I'd honestly prefer for someone else to make that call.
She's waiting for the paint to dry before she pulls the tape.
For a first attempt to go that smoothly is genuinely unusual.
There's no reason for us to leave this early.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause)
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb of telling or knowing] how that [clause]. · [subject] [verb of telling] [indirect object] how that [clause]. · [imperative verb] how that [clause]. · [subject] [verb of writing or saying] how that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma before how that, none between how and that, and none inside the clause. Modern American English uses a plain that or a plain how, never the pair.
variants: how alone in narrative use (He told us how he'd walked all night)
entries.meaning: A doubled complementizer common in Early Modern English and preserved in the King James Bible, where how had drifted away from manner and become a bare statement-marker. It is dead in contemporary American English except as deliberate period flavor; the modern equivalent of He told them how that the ship had gone down is simply He told them that the ship had gone down.
examples: Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man of my nation to keep company with a stranger.
He told them how that the ship had gone down within sight of the harbor.
Remember how that our fathers came into this country with nothing at all.
The old preacher explained how that mercy is never earned.
She wrote how that the winter had been the hardest in living memory.

entries.type: complementizer after verbs of fearing; subordinating (negative purpose) elsewhere
entries.clause: noun clause after a verb, adjective, or noun of fearing; adverbial clause of negative purpose otherwise
entries.pattern: [subject] [verb of fearing] lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb]. · [subject] be [adjective of fearing] lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb]. · [noun of fearing] lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb]. · [main clause] lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb]. · [main clause], lest [subject] [bare subjunctive verb].
entries.punctuation: No comma before lest in the noun-clause use — it sits between a verb, adjective, or noun and its own complement. In the purpose use a comma is optional and usually omitted; use one only when the lest clause is a clearly parenthetical afterthought. Lest never fronts in either use, so the fronted-subordinator comma never applies to it.
variants: lest + should (lest he should fall) — dated, and more British than American
entries.meaning: A negative complementizer meaning roughly "that … might," used after fear, afraid, anxious, worry, and apprehension: She feared lest the news get out means "feared that the news might get out." It takes the bare subjunctive — lest he be, lest it go, with no -s on a third-person verb — and that is the detail Americans most often get wrong. It is never neutral; ordinary American speech uses that … might or for fear that.
examples: He was afraid lest his silence be taken for agreement.
The family lived in fear lest the loan be called in.
She hesitated, anxious lest she say the wrong thing.
Speak quietly lest the neighbors hear you.
The committee worried lest the delay cost them the grant.
He kept every receipt in a folder, lest anyone question the expense later.

entries.term: no wonder / small wonder / little wonder
entries.respell: noh WUN-dur, smawl WUN-dur, LIT-l WUN-dur
entries.type: complementizer frame (reduced matrix predicate); the unreduced form is It is no wonder that
entries.register: no wonder neutral to informal; small wonder and little wonder neutral to formal, and commoner on the page than in the mouth
entries.clause: noun clause (extraposed subject content clause), normally with the that dropped
entries.pattern: No wonder ∅ [clause]. · No wonder that [clause]. · It is no wonder that [clause]. · [main clause] — no wonder ∅ [clause]. · Small wonder that [clause]. · Little wonder ∅ [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the frame and its clause: No wonder he was tired, not No wonder, he was tired. When it trails a complete sentence it needs a period, a semicolon, or a dash in front of it — The heater's been off since Friday; no wonder the pipes froze — because both halves are independent clauses and a comma there is a comma splice.
variants: the unreduced It's no wonder that
is it any wonder (that) in questions
no surprise, small surprise — the same frame with a different noun
entries.meaning: A whole matrix clause squeezed down to two words: It is no wonder that he was tired drops it is and that and comes out No wonder he was tired, with the content clause still doing the work of a subject. That reduction is what makes it look like a conjunction, and the proof that it still is one is that the full form can always be put back. Small wonder and little wonder mean the same thing in a more written register; only no wonder is at home in speech, and only no wonder stands alone as an exclamation (No wonder!).
examples: No wonder the car wouldn't start — the dome light had been on all night.
Small wonder that enrollment fell the year they doubled the fee.
She's been up since four with the baby. No wonder she fell asleep at the table.
Little wonder the neighbors finally called the city about the noise.
They cut the staff in half and kept the same hours; no wonder the rest of them quit.
It's no wonder that nobody reads the terms of service.
related: trouble is / problem is / fact is / truth is

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.clause: noun clause, negated — parenthetical, or a denial of an inference
entries.pattern: Not that [clause], but [main clause]. · [main clause] — not that [clause]. · It's not that [clause]; it's that [clause]. · Not that [clause].
entries.punctuation: When it opens the sentence, a comma closes its clause before the main clause arrives: Not that it matters, but he left early. When it trails, it needs a comma, a dash, or a full sentence break in front of it: He never returned the call — not that I expected him to. In the It's not that X; it's that Y frame the two halves are both independent clauses, so a semicolon (or a period, or a dash) is required between them; a comma there is a comma splice, common in casual writing and still an error in edited prose.
variants: the fixed phrases not that it matters, not that I'm complaining, not that I know of
entries.meaning: A complementizer that denies an inference the listener might be drawing — usually right before the speaker goes ahead and makes the point anyway. In the It's not that … it's that … frame it does the more literal work of rejecting one that-clause in favor of another. It is one of the few environments where the that cannot be dropped.
examples: Not that anyone asked, but I thought the second draft was better.
He never returned the call — not that I expected him to.
It's not that I don't trust her; it's that I don't trust the process.
Not that it matters now, but the reservation was under my name.
"Is he still working there?" "Not that I know of."

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal)
entries.clause: noun clause (nominalized content clause)
entries.pattern: The fact that [clause] [verb phrase]. · [preposition] the fact that [clause]. · [verb] the fact that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma anywhere in the phrase and none between that and its clause. Never drop this that — after a noun the complementizer is obligatory.
variants: the fact of the matter is that
the same frame with other nouns — the idea that, the claim that, the possibility that, the news that
entries.meaning: A packaging device that turns a clause into a full noun phrase so it can follow a preposition or head a sentence, since a bare that-clause cannot do either after most prepositions: despite that he lied is ungrammatical, despite the fact that he lied is fine. Editors flag it as padding wherever a plain that-clause or a gerund would carry the same load — I resent the fact that he lied shrinks cleanly to I resent that he lied.
examples: The fact that nobody objected doesn't make it legal.
They settled despite the fact that liability was never established.
She kept coming back to the fact that the door had been unlocked.
The fact that he apologized at all surprised everyone in the room.
We're stuck with the fact that the deadline hasn't moved an inch.
related: the idea that / the notion that / the claim that

entries.term: the idea that / the notion that / the claim that
entries.ipa: /ði aɪˈdiə ðət/, /ðə ˈnoʊʃən ðət/, /ðə ˈkleɪm ðət/
entries.respell: thee eye-DEE-uh thut, thuh NOH-shun thut, thuh KLAYM thut
entries.type: complementizer (phrasal — abstract noun + that)
entries.clause: noun clause (appositive content clause completing an abstract noun)
entries.pattern: The [noun] that [clause] [verb phrase]. · [verb] the [noun] that [clause]. · [preposition] the [noun] that [clause]. · [determiner] [noun] that [clause]. · The [noun] that [clause] is [complement].
entries.punctuation: No comma between the noun and that, and none between that and its clause. This that can never be dropped — the claim he was misquoted reads as a relative clause with a hole in it, which is a different sentence. And no comma before the verb even when the whole phrase is the subject: The notion that anyone reads these surprises me.
variants: the same frame with any abstract noun that takes a content clause — the fact that, the possibility that, the belief that, the news that, the rumor that, the assumption that, the suggestion that
the interrogative counterpart the question whether
entries.meaning: The productive frame behind the fact that: an abstract noun naming a piece of mental content — idea, notion, claim, belief, rumor, possibility — takes a that-clause that says what the content is. The clause is appositive, not relative, and the test is substitution rather than deletion: the claim that he was misquoted means "the claim, namely that he was misquoted," and nothing has been lifted out of the clause. Compare the claim that he made, where that is a relative pronoun standing in for the object of made and can be deleted. The choice among the nouns is attitude, not structure — the fact that concedes the content is true, the idea that and the notion that usually telegraph doubt, and the claim that withholds endorsement outright.
examples: The idea that one more meeting will fix this is optimistic at best.
She rejected the notion that the delay was anybody's fault but the vendor's.
The claim that the road was already flooded turned out to be wrong.
Everything rests on the assumption that the grant gets renewed.
We spent the afternoon with the possibility that the offer might be pulled.
The rumor that the plant is closing has been going around since March.
He never quite let go of the belief that the inspection had been rigged.

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal — noun + whether)
entries.register: formal — legal, academic, and editorial prose
entries.clause: noun clause (appositive indirect yes-no question completing an abstract noun)
entries.pattern: The question whether [clause] [verb phrase]. · [verb] the question whether [clause]. · [preposition] the question of whether [clause]. · The question whether to [verb]. · The question whether [clause] or [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between question and whether, none inside the clause, and none after the whole phrase when it is the sentence's subject: The question whether the statute applies has never been briefed. Never the question that — a yes-no question takes whether, and never the question if, since an if-clause cannot follow a noun at all.
variants: the question of whether — commoner in American English and perfectly acceptable, only a little heavier
the question as to whether (see as to whether)
the same frame with other nouns — the issue whether, a doubt whether, a dispute whether
entries.meaning: The interrogative counterpart of the idea that: when the abstract noun names an open question instead of a settled content, whether replaces that. Bare the question whether is the traditional legal form and is still standard; American usage more often slips in of, and that of is not an error. The question as to whether is the same phrase with a third word most editors strike. The one form to avoid entirely is the question if.
examples: The question whether the easement survives the sale has never been litigated.
The board tabled the question whether to reopen the north entrance.
Everything now turns on the question of whether the notice was timely.
The question whether he knew is separate from the question whether he should have.
She raised the question whether the committee had jurisdiction at all.
The question whether the fee is refundable or forfeited is buried in an appendix.
related: the idea that / the notion that / the claim that

entries.term: the thing is / here's the thing
entries.respell: thuh THING iz, heerz thuh THING
entries.type: complementizer frame (specificational be + content clause); here's the thing is the same frame turned into a discourse marker
entries.register: informal — ordinary in speech, dialogue, and conversational writing; out of place in formal prose
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause) as subject complement, normally with the that dropped
entries.pattern: The thing is ∅ [clause]. · The thing is, ∅ [clause]. · The thing is that [clause]. · Here's the thing: [clause]. · Here's the thing — [clause]. · [main clause], but the thing is ∅ [clause].
entries.punctuation: This is one of the two frames in the section that regularly takes a comma at the junction, and it is not the usual complementizer error: the comma stands for the pause after is and is standard in edited dialogue (The thing is, nobody asked her). Put the that back in and the comma goes away (The thing is that nobody asked her). Here's the thing takes a colon, a dash, or a period after it — never a bare comma, which would splice two independent clauses.
variants: trouble is / problem is / fact is / truth is — the article-dropping members of the same family
the thing about it is
here's the thing about + noun phrase
entries.meaning: A specificational sentence doing duty as a conversational hinge: the thing is an empty placeholder noun and the clause after is supplies its content. What it actually signals is that a complication is coming — The thing is almost always introduces the catch, the objection, or the reason the previous suggestion will not work. Here's the thing makes the same move with the placeholder pushed to the front, announcing the complication a beat before naming it. Neither belongs in formal writing, where the sentence gets stated without the runway.
examples: The thing is, nobody actually told the landlord we were subletting.
Here's the thing: the warranty ran out two months before it broke.
I'd love to help, but the thing is I'm already committed Saturday.
The thing is that the part is discontinued, not just backordered.
Here's the thing — she never signed the second page.
He kept promising to pay us back. The thing is, he never did.
related: trouble is / problem is / fact is / truth is

entries.term: trouble is / problem is / fact is / truth is
entries.respell: TRUB-l iz, PRAH-blum iz, FAKT iz, TROOTH iz
entries.type: complementizer frame (specificational be + content clause, with the article dropped)
entries.register: informal to neutral — the article-less form is conversational; restoring the makes any of them fit edited prose
entries.clause: noun clause (declarative content clause) as subject complement, normally with the that dropped
entries.pattern: Trouble is ∅ [clause]. · Fact is, ∅ [clause]. · The trouble is that [clause]. · [main clause], but the problem is ∅ [clause]. · Truth is, ∅ [clause], and [clause].
entries.punctuation: A comma after is is standard wherever the pause is real (Fact is, nobody checked), and no comma at all when the sentence runs straight through (The trouble is nobody checked). With an overt that there is never a comma. When one of these follows a complete sentence it needs a period, a semicolon, or a dash in front of it, since both halves are independent: We budgeted for three months; trouble is, the permit took five.
variants: the full forms the trouble is, the problem is, the fact is, the truth is
the thing is / here's the thing
thing is, point is
question is — the interrogative member, which takes whether rather than that
entries.meaning: The same specificational frame as the thing is with the article knocked off the front, which is a real feature of American conversational syntax rather than carelessness: Trouble is, the permit took five months is a fixed pattern, not a typo for The trouble is. Dropping the is what marks the register, and putting it back is the entire fix when the sentence has to go into formal writing. The four nouns do not carry equal force — trouble is and problem is introduce an obstacle, while fact is and truth is introduce a correction the listener is expected to resist.
examples: Trouble is, the permit took five months instead of three.
Fact is, nobody on that shift had been trained on the new machine.
We could repaint it, but the problem is the trim would still be wrong.
Truth is, I'd forgotten the whole conversation until she brought it up.
The trouble is that the replacement costs more than the repair.
Everyone keeps blaming the storm. Fact is, the roof was already failing.
He says the check is in the mail; truth is, he hasn't written it yet.
related: the thing is / here's the thing
no wonder / small wonder / little wonder

entries.type: complementizer (phrasal, optative) — the fossilized remains of I would that
entries.register: archaic and literary — poetry, elevated rhetoric, and deliberate period voice; never a neutral choice
entries.clause: noun clause (content clause expressing a wish), verb in the past subjunctive
entries.pattern: Would that [subject] [past subjunctive verb]. · Would that [subject] were [complement]. · Would that [subject] had [past participle]. · Would that [clause], [main clause]. · Would to God that [clause].
entries.punctuation: No comma between would and that, and none before the clause. The sentence it heads is an exclamation of wish and takes a period or an exclamation point, never a question mark, despite the inverted look of the leading would. If a main clause follows, a comma closes the wish first: Would that it were true, but the numbers say otherwise.
variants: would that with the that dropped (Would it were so)
would to God that
the living paraphrases if only and I wish
entries.meaning: An optative frame: would is the old volitional verb meaning "wish" with its subject worn away, and that is the ordinary complementizer introducing the thing wished for. It takes the past subjunctive — were, not was, and had plus a participle for a wish about the past — and the tense is counterfactual, so Would that it were true says outright that it is not. Modern American English says If only it were true or I wish it were true; would that survives in speech only as a set piece of raised-eyebrow formality.
examples: Would that it were as simple as signing one form.
Would that he had said so before we bought the tickets.
Would that the two sides could agree on even the basic facts.
Would that I had listened to my sister about the roof.
Would that the world were run by people who read the reports.
Would that it were true, but the numbers say otherwise.
